newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire says it will recapture areas lost to rebels.
newsitem.headline: Zaire says it will recapture areas lost to rebels.

text.p: Zaire's army chief said on Saturday he now had the means to recapture a swathe of eastern Zaire under rebel control.

A presidential adviser, meanwhile, said that Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo would hold talks in France on Saturday with ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, who is recuperating after cancer surgery in Switzerland but says he will return home.
"We have lost the battle, not the war," state radio quoted Army Chief of Staff General Eluki Monga as saying.
The radio quoted Eluki, who is himself in the east, as saying that the government had put everything at the disposal of the army for it to recapture the lost territory.

Zairean deputy Foreign Minister Lokondo Yoka, speaking in Brussels on Friday, accused neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi's Tutsi-dominated armies of occupying the eastern towns of Uvira, Bukavu and Goma. "We are determined to wage a total war...We have the means," he said.
The revolt in the east of the sprawling, chaotic and corruption-plagued nation is the latest manifestation of pressures threatening to tear the former Belgian colony apart.

Earlier this month, Eluki accused the government of part-Tutsi Prime Minister Kengo of not giving the army the means to defend the country against the rebels, a coalition of ethnic Tutsis and other opponents of Mobutu.

Mobutu adviser Honore Ngbanda told Reuters the president, who seized power in a 1965 coup, would return soon to Zaire but he gave no precise date. "As things stand, Mobutu will come back to Kinshasa and take things back into his hands," he said.
Mobutu is the one symbol of national unity in a country where individual regions such as copper-rich Shaba and diamond-rich Kasai enjoy de facto autonomy.

Taking advantage of superpower rivalry, he ruled virtually unchallenged from 1965 until foreign and domestic pressure forced him to embrace multi-party politics in 1990. Elections, repeatedly postponed, are promised by July 1997.

Zaire's eastern border provinces of North and South Kivu have been host to over a million Rwandan Hutu refugees who fled in fear of reprisals after Hutu hardliners massacred hundreds of thousands of minority Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994.
As many of 700,000 refugees near Goma began an unexpected exodus to Rwanda on Friday as preparations for despatch of a multinational force to provide humanitarion aid took shape.
But hundreds of thousands of others plus fleeing armed Hutu hardliners are scattered in forests and hills deeper in Zaire.
Retreating from the battle front Zaire's ragged army has left a trail of robbery and destruction in its wake as it tries to live off the land.
Officials said Eluki went last week to Kindu, 300 km (190 miles) west of Bukavu, where many retreating soldiers have been regrouped and joined by fresh troops flown from Kinshasa.
Traditional celebrations to mark National Army Day, which usually include military parades, were cancelled on Saturday.
"We are in a state of war," an army spokesman said.
